Consistency.justification: The proposal aligns strongly with the deployment-aware intent of the research idea. It adopts the interface-attention-alignment taxonomy, covers classical and modern fusion families, couples image-fidelity metrics with downstream accuracy and system costs, and includes the requested guidance on temporal consistency, robustness, efficiency, and physics-grounded interpretation. The experiments also operationalize the proposed comparison-to-deployment protocol. The main inconsistency is one of emphasis: the stated idea is principally a comprehensive review and synthesis, whereas the proposal evolves into a large empirical benchmarking and algorithm-development project. The review methodology itself, including literature search strategy, inclusion criteria, coverage of dynamic methods, and procedures for taxonomy validation, is not specified. Thus, it is highly consistent with the technical themes but not perfectly aligned with the review-centered form of the original idea.

Clarity.justification: The motivation, high-level hypothesis, contributions, experiment categories, metrics, and anticipated artifacts are presented in a logical and understandable manner. The proposal clearly distinguishes benchmark construction, task-aware training, temporal regularization, physics-guided modeling, compression, and statistical evaluation. However, several important definitions remain underspecified. The interface-attention-alignment taxonomy is named but not formally defined; the exact formulation of each loss is absent; energy measurement procedures and target hardware are vague; and the proposed multi-objective score lacks a precise normalization rule. It is also unclear how datasets with different annotations, resolutions, registration quality, and temporal properties will be harmonized. These ambiguities prevent the proposal from being fully reproducible as written.

Novelty.justification: The strongest originality lies in integrating fidelity, downstream task utility, robustness curves, temporal behavior, and deployment costs into one reproducible IR-VIS evaluation framework. A standardized recipe book and cross-architecture analysis could be a useful contribution, particularly if it reveals reliable reversals between fidelity rankings and task rankings. Nevertheless, most individual components are established ideas: task-aware perceptual or feature losses, frozen task networks, temporal consistency through optical flow, contrastive temporal learning, quantization-aware training, pruning, controlled corruptions, and Pareto-front analysis are all common in adjacent multimodal perception fields. The physics-guided disentanglement component could add novelty, but its current formulation is too preliminary to establish a distinct technical advance. The proposal appropriately acknowledges that its novelty is primarily integrative and empirical rather than methodological.

Soundness.justification: The overall empirical structure is reasonable: representative baselines, controlled corruption sweeps, downstream evaluation, temporal analysis, compression studies, ablations, multiple seeds, confidence intervals, and robustness summaries provide a credible foundation. Important methodological issues remain unresolved. Fidelity metrics such as PSNR and SSIM are difficult to interpret for fusion when no unique ground-truth fused image exists, and the proposal does not state how reference targets will be selected. Simulated fog, rain, misregistration, thermal drift, and emissivity changes may not reproduce the joint statistics of real sensor failures, so conclusions about deployment robustness require validation on naturally degraded data. Frozen task heads can introduce proxy-model bias and may reward detector-specific artifacts rather than generally useful fusion. The proposed emissivity constraint is physically oversimplified because measured infrared radiance depends on temperature, wavelength, atmospheric transmission, reflected ambient radiation, sensor response, and material emissivity; simply scaling a learned emission map by emissivity does not identify thermal emission or visible reflectance. The evaluation also needs explicit scene-level resampling, multiple-comparison controls, calibration procedures, fair input-resolution and hardware settings, and cross-dataset testing. These are substantial but repairable rigor issues.

Feasibility.justification: Most components can be implemented using public datasets, existing fusion models, standard corruption libraries, established task networks, optical-flow estimators, and common edge-optimization tools. Releasing code and beginning with a compact baseline set are practical choices. However, the full scope is ambitious: it spans several heterogeneous datasets, five broad model families, detection and segmentation, video evaluation, multiple degradations and severity levels, multiple task heads and seeds, temporal models, physics-guided training, pruning, quantization, and hardware profiling. KAIST, FLIR, and TNO differ considerably in registration, spectral characteristics, annotations, licenses, and availability of temporal sequences; TNO in particular is not naturally suited to all proposed downstream and temporal tests. Reliable energy measurement also requires specified devices, synchronized instrumentation, warm-up and power protocols, and control of preprocessing costs. Completing all combinations rigorously would demand substantial compute, engineering, annotation work, and hardware access, so prioritization and a staged execution plan are needed.

Significance.justification: The proposal addresses an important gap between image-fusion papers optimized for conventional visual metrics and real systems that care about perception accuracy, robustness, latency, memory, energy, and temporal stability. A credible standardized benchmark could improve model selection, discourage misleading metric-only claims, and guide deployment on autonomous, surveillance, robotics, and safety-related platforms. Public code, measurement protocols, Pareto analyses, and robustness audits could have broad practical value. The likely impact is meaningful rather than transformative because benchmark adoption is uncertain, simulated degradations may limit external validity, and conclusions may depend on selected task heads, datasets, and hardware. Its significance would increase considerably with real-world corruption data, standardized energy protocols, and evidence that findings generalize across sensors and tasks.

strengths: Strongly connects fusion quality to downstream perception, robustness, temporal stability, and deployment costs through a coherent benchmark-oriented agenda.
Proposes useful community artifacts, including standardized protocols, reproducible code, Pareto frontiers, robustness audits, compression guidance, and cross-architecture ablations.
Explicitly recognizes major limitations such as dataset heterogeneity, detector dependence, computational cost, and the incremental nature of the algorithmic components.
weaknesses: The proposal shifts from the requested comprehensive review toward a much broader benchmark and algorithm-development project without specifying a systematic review methodology.
The physics-guided emissivity formulation is oversimplified and potentially non-identifiable, requiring a more defensible image-formation model or substantially narrower claims.

Evaluation details needed for rigorous comparison are missing, including reference-free treatment of fusion quality, real-corruption validation, dataset harmonization, energy measurement protocols, statistical units, and controls for task-head bias.
The experimental matrix is very large relative to the stated plan and will likely require staged prioritization, additional annotations, substantial compute, and access to standardized edge hardware.
